questions.stem: In the Brønsted-Lowry model, what does an acid do when it reacts with a base?
options: It donates a pair of electrons to the base
It releases hydroxide ions into the water
It donates a proton (H⁺) to the base
It accepts a proton (H⁺) from the base
questions.explanation: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Releasing hydroxide ions describes a base in the older Arrhenius model.

questions.stem: What is the conjugate base of the hydrogen sulfate ion, HSO₄⁻?
options: H₂SO₄
SO₃²⁻
OH⁻
SO₄²⁻
questions.explanation: A conjugate base is what remains after an acid loses one proton: HSO₄⁻ → SO₄²⁻ + H⁺. H₂SO₄ is the conjugate acid of HSO₄⁻, formed by gaining a proton.

questions.stem: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). Which species acts as a Brønsted-Lowry acid in the forward reaction?
options: NH₄⁺
OH⁻
H₂O
NH₃
questions.explanation: Water donates a proton to ammonia, forming OH⁻, so water is the acid in the forward reaction. NH₄⁺ is an acid only in the reverse reaction, where it gives a proton back to OH⁻.

questions.stem: HNO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NO₂⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). Which are the two conjugate acid-base pairs?
options: HNO₂/H₂O and NO₂⁻/H₃O⁺
HNO₂/NO₂⁻ and H₂O/OH⁻
HNO₂/NO₂⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O
HNO₂/H₃O⁺ and NO₂⁻/H₂O
questions.explanation: Members of a conjugate pair differ by exactly one proton. HNO₂ loses a proton to become NO₂⁻, and H₂O gains one to become H₃O⁺. OH⁻ does not appear in this equation.

questions.stem: Water acts as a base when it reacts with HCl and as an acid when it reacts with NH₃. What term describes a species that can do both?
options: Polyprotic
Monoprotic
Neutral
Amphiprotic
questions.explanation: An amphiprotic species can either donate or accept a proton, depending on what it reacts with. Polyprotic describes an acid that can donate more than one proton per molecule.

questions.stem: Which of these acids is diprotic?
options: Hydrochloric acid, HCl
Nitric acid, HNO₃
Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH
Sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄
questions.explanation: Each H₂SO₄ molecule can donate two protons. HCl, HNO₃ and ethanoic acid are monoprotic; in ethanoic acid only the hydrogen of the -COOH group is donated.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the first ionisation of phosphoric acid in water?
options: H₃PO₄(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
H₃PO₄(aq) → PO₄³⁻(aq) + 3H⁺(aq)
H₃PO₄(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₄PO₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HPO₄²⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
questions.explanation: A polyprotic acid ionises one proton at a time, and phosphoric acid is weak, so each step is an equilibrium. The step forming HPO₄²⁻ is the second ionisation, and losing all three protons at once does not happen.

questions.stem: How many moles of sodium hydroxide are needed to neutralise 0.010 mol of sulfuric acid completely?
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Sulfuric acid is diprotic, so it needs two moles of hydroxide for each mole of acid. 0.010 mol would be right only for a monoprotic acid.

questions.stem: For a polyprotic acid, each successive Ka is much smaller than the one before. Why?
options: The water molecules are used up by the first ionisation, so fewer remain
It is harder to remove a positive proton from an increasingly negative ion
Each proton removed makes the remaining ion more positive, so it repels H⁺
The later protons are bonded to oxygen, but the first is bonded to hydrogen
questions.explanation: After the first proton leaves, the species carries a negative charge, which attracts the next proton more strongly; each further step is harder still. In phosphoric acid all three ionisable hydrogens are bonded to oxygen.

questions.stem: Nitric acid is classed as a strong acid. What does 'strong' mean here?
options: It ionises almost completely in aqueous solution
It is present at a high concentration in solution
It can donate more than one proton per molecule
It reacts with metals to produce hydrogen gas
questions.explanation: Strength describes the degree of ionisation at equilibrium. Concentration is the amount of acid per litre, and the number of protons donated per molecule describes whether it is monoprotic or polyprotic.

questions.stem: One bottle holds 10 mol/L ethanoic acid and another holds 0.010 mol/L hydrochloric acid. Which statement is correct?
options: Both acids are strong, because both turn blue litmus paper red in solution
The ethanoic acid is concentrated but weak; the hydrochloric acid is dilute but strong
The ethanoic acid is concentrated and strong; the hydrochloric acid is dilute and weak
The ethanoic acid is dilute but strong; the hydrochloric acid is concentrated but weak
questions.explanation: Concentration and strength are separate ideas. Ethanoic acid ionises only slightly whatever its concentration, while HCl ionises almost completely even when dilute.

questions.stem: Which equation correctly represents ethanoic acid, a weak acid, in water?
options: CH₃COOH(aq) → CH₃⁺(aq) + COOH⁻(aq)
CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH₂⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
questions.explanation: A weak acid ionises only partly, so its ionisation is an equilibrium, shown with ⇌. A single arrow is used for strong acids, which ionise almost completely.

questions.stem: What is the acidity constant expression for hydrocyanic acid: HCN(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + CN⁻(aq)?
options: Ka = [HCN] / ([H₃O⁺][CN⁻])
Ka = [H₃O⁺][CN⁻] / ([HCN][H₂O])
Ka = [H₃O⁺] + [CN⁻] - [HCN]
Ka = [H₃O⁺][CN⁻] / [HCN]
questions.explanation: Products go over reactants. Water is the solvent and its concentration is effectively constant, so it is left out of Ka. The inverted expression would be the constant for the reverse reaction.

questions.stem: Four weak monoprotic acids have Ka values: HW 1.8 x 10⁻⁴, HX 1.7 x 10⁻⁵, HY 3.0 x 10⁻⁸, HZ 6.2 x 10⁻¹⁰. Solutions of each at 0.10 mol/L are prepared. Which has the lowest pH?
options: HZ
HW
HX
HY
questions.explanation: The larger Ka is, the further the ionisation equilibrium lies to the right and the higher [H₃O⁺], so the lower the pH. HZ, with the smallest Ka, is the weakest acid and has the highest pH.

questions.stem: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and hydrocyanic acid (Ka = 6.2 x 10⁻¹⁰) are both 0.10 mol/L. Which statement is correct?
options: Equal volumes have the same [H₃O⁺], but HCN neutralises far less NaOH
HCN neutralises more NaOH, because its molecules hold their protons more tightly
Neither neutralises NaOH completely, because both are present at low concentration
Equal volumes neutralise the same amount of NaOH, but HCN has a far lower [H₃O⁺]
questions.explanation: Both contain 0.10 mol of acid per litre, and as OH⁻ removes H₃O⁺ the HCN equilibrium keeps shifting right, so they neutralise the same amount of base. Only the free [H₃O⁺], and so the pH, differs.

questions.stem: A 0.20 mol/L solution of a weak monoprotic acid HA has a pH of 3.00. Assuming [HA] at equilibrium is about 0.20 mol/L, what is Ka?
questions.explanation: [H₃O⁺] = [A⁻] = 10⁻³ mol/L, so Ka = (1.0 x 10⁻³)² / 0.20 = 5.0 x 10⁻⁶. Forgetting to square gives 5.0 x 10⁻³, and 1.0 x 10⁻³ is just [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: A solution of a weak acid is diluted with water. What happens to the percentage of acid molecules that are ionised?
options: It decreases, because there are fewer acid molecules in each litre
It stays the same, because Ka does not change with concentration
It falls to zero, because water reacts with the ions formed
It increases, because dilution favours the side with more dissolved particles
questions.explanation: HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻ has two dissolved particles on the right and one on the left, so dilution shifts it right and a larger fraction ionises. Ka is unchanged, but the position shifts; [H₃O⁺] still falls overall.

questions.stem: Which expression and value for the ionisation constant of water, Kw, are correct at 25 °C?
options: Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 x 10⁻¹⁴
Kw = [H₃O⁺] + [OH⁻] = 1.0 x 10⁻¹⁴
Kw = [H₃O⁺] / [OH⁻] = 1.0 x 10⁻¹⁴
questions.explanation: Water self-ionises: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻, with Kw equal to the product of the two ion concentrations, 1.0 x 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C. In pure water each ion is 1.0 x 10⁻⁷ mol/L.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.020 mol/L hydrochloric acid at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: HCl ionises completely, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.020 mol/L and pH = -log(0.020) = 1.70. 12.30 is the pH of 0.020 mol/L NaOH.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.0010 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: [OH⁻] = 1.0 x 10⁻³ mol/L, so [H₃O⁺] = Kw / [OH⁻] = 1.0 x 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 x 10⁻³ = 1.0 x 10⁻¹¹ mol/L and pH = 11.0. 3.0 is -log[OH⁻], not the pH.

questions.stem: A sample of rainwater has a pH of 4.5. What is its hydrogen ion concentration?
options: 4.5 x 10⁻⁵ mol/L
3.2 x 10⁻⁴ mol/L
4.5 mol/L
3.2 x 10⁻⁵ mol/L
questions.explanation: [H₃O⁺] = 10^(-pH) = 10^(-4.5) = 3.2 x 10⁻⁵ mol/L. The pH is a logarithm, so it is not simply the number in front of a power of ten.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.0050 mol/L calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, at 25 °C? Assume it dissolves and dissociates completely.
questions.explanation: Each Ca(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.010 mol/L and [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 x 10⁻¹⁴ / 0.010 = 1.0 x 10⁻¹² mol/L, giving pH 12.0. Forgetting the factor of two gives 11.7.

questions.stem: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 4.0 x 10⁻⁹ mol/L at 25 °C. What is [OH⁻]?
options: 4.0 x 10⁻⁵ mol/L
1.0 x 10⁻⁷ mol/L
2.5 x 10⁻⁵ mol/L
2.5 x 10⁻⁶ mol/L
questions.explanation: [OH⁻] = Kw / [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 x 10⁻¹⁴ / 4.0 x 10⁻⁹ = 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ mol/L, so the solution is basic. 1.0 x 10⁻⁷ mol/L applies only to a neutral solution.

questions.stem: At 50 °C, Kw = 5.5 x 10⁻¹⁴ and pure water has a pH of about 6.6. Which statement is correct?
options: The water is neutral, because [H₃O⁺] still equals [OH⁻]
The water is acidic, because its pH is below 7
The water is basic, because Kw has become larger
The water is acidic, because heating adds H₃O⁺ ions
questions.explanation: Self-ionisation of water is endothermic, so heating increases both [H₃O⁺] and [OH⁻] equally and the pH falls. Neutral means [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻], which equals pH 7 only at 25 °C.

questions.stem: 50.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.060 mol/L NaOH. What is the pH of the mixture?
questions.explanation: n(H₃O⁺) = 0.00500 mol and n(OH⁻) = 0.00300 mol, leaving 0.00200 mol H₃O⁺ in 0.100 L, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.0200 mol/L and pH = 1.70. Using 50.0 mL instead of the total volume gives 1.40.

questions.stem: Why does an acid-base indicator change colour as pH changes?
options: It is a strong acid that is destroyed when the solution becomes basic
It reacts with water at pH 7 to form a coloured precipitate
It absorbs hydroxide ions, which are coloured in solution
It is a weak acid whose acid form and conjugate base differ in colour
questions.explanation: An indicator HIn is in equilibrium with In⁻; changing [H₃O⁺] shifts the position, so the colour of whichever form is more abundant is seen. Hydroxide ions themselves are colourless.

questions.stem: Methyl orange, HIn, is red and its conjugate base, In⁻, is yellow: HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻. Why does a yellow solution of methyl orange turn red when acid is added?
options: Added H⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the right, forming more red In⁻
Added acid destroys the yellow In⁻, leaving only colourless water
Added acid raises the temperature, which makes the indicator red
Added H⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the left, forming more red HIn
questions.explanation: Increasing [H⁺] increases the rate of the reverse reaction, so the position shifts left and red HIn dominates. In basic solution H⁺ is removed, so the equilibrium shifts right and yellow In⁻ dominates.

questions.stem: Indicator ranges: methyl orange 3.1-4.4, methyl red 4.4-6.2, bromothymol blue 6.0-7.6, phenolphthalein 8.3-10.0. Ammonia solution is titrated with hydrochloric acid, and the equivalence point is at about pH 5.3. Which indicator is most suitable?
options: Bromothymol blue
Phenolphthalein
Methyl red
Methyl orange
questions.explanation: A suitable indicator changes colour over a range that includes the equivalence point pH. Only methyl red's range (4.4-6.2) contains pH 5.3; phenolphthalein would change well before equivalence.

questions.stem: Why is universal indicator not used to find the end point of a titration?
options: It changes colour gradually over a wide pH range, so there is no sharp end point
It changes colour only at exactly pH 7, which few equivalence points reach
It reacts with the titrant, so it can be used only in unbuffered solutions
It is colourless in both acids and bases, so no change can be seen
questions.explanation: Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators that shows many colours across the pH scale, which is useful for estimating pH but gives no single, sudden colour change at equivalence.

questions.stem: Why are only two or three drops of indicator added in a titration?
options: The indicator is itself a weak acid, so a large amount would react with the titrant
The indicator is a strong base, so a large amount would neutralise all of the acid
A large amount of indicator would raise Kw, changing the pH at equivalence
A large amount of indicator would make the solution too dark to see the burette
questions.explanation: Indicators are weak acids or bases, so they consume a little of the titrant. Using only a few drops keeps this error negligible while still giving a clear colour change.

questions.stem: In an acid-base titration, what is the equivalence point?
options: The point where the indicator first shows a permanent colour change
The point where the pH of the solution in the flask is exactly 7
The point where equal volumes of acid and base have been added
The point where acid and base have reacted in the mole ratio of the equation
questions.explanation: At equivalence the reactants have been mixed in exactly stoichiometric amounts. The end point is where the indicator changes colour, chosen to be as close as possible to equivalence; the equivalence pH is 7 only for a strong acid with a strong base.

questions.stem: A pH meter is used instead of an indicator, and pH is plotted against the volume of base added. How is the equivalence point identified?
options: At the point where the curve levels off after all the base is added
At whichever volume gives a pH reading of exactly 7.0
At the middle of the steep, nearly vertical section of the curve
At the point where the curve first starts to rise from its start
questions.explanation: Near equivalence a tiny volume of base causes a large jump in pH, and the equivalence point lies at the midpoint of that steep rise. It is at pH 7 only for strong acid-strong base titrations.

questions.stem: A 20.00 mL aliquot of sodium hydroxide solution needs 16.40 mL of 0.1000 mol/L hydrochloric acid to reach the end point. What is the concentration of the NaOH?
questions.explanation: n(HCl) = 0.1000 x 0.01640 = 0.001640 mol, which equals n(NaOH) by the 1 : 1 ratio; c = 0.001640 / 0.02000 = 0.08200 mol/L. 0.1220 mol/L comes from swapping the two volumes.

questions.stem: A 25.00 mL aliquot of sulfuric acid is titrated with 0.1250 mol/L NaOH, and the average titre is 21.60 mL. What is the concentration of the sulfuric acid?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.1250 x 0.02160 = 0.002700 mol. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, so n(H₂SO₄) = 0.001350 mol and c = 0.001350 / 0.02500 = 0.05400 mol/L. Ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio gives 0.1080 mol/L.

questions.stem: Which rinsing procedure is correct before a titration?
options: Burette, pipette and conical flask all with distilled water only
Burette and pipette with distilled water; conical flask with the titrant
Burette, pipette and conical flask all with the solutions they will hold
Burette and pipette with the solutions they deliver; conical flask with distilled water
questions.explanation: Water left in the burette or pipette would dilute the solution delivered, so they are rinsed with that solution. Water in the flask does not change the amount of substance in the aliquot, but rinsing it with the aliquot solution would add extra.

questions.stem: Titres recorded: 23.80 mL (rough), 22.65 mL, 22.70 mL, 22.60 mL and 23.10 mL. Which average titre should be used?
options: 22.76 mL, from all four accurate titres
22.97 mL, from all five titres recorded
23.10 mL, the largest accurate titre
22.65 mL, from the three concordant titres
questions.explanation: Concordant titres agree within about 0.10 mL, so 22.65, 22.70 and 22.60 mL are averaged to 22.65 mL. The rough titre and the outlying 23.10 mL are left out.

questions.stem: Anhydrous sodium carbonate, not sodium hydroxide, is used to make a primary standard solution. Why?
options: Sodium carbonate is a strong acid, so it gives a sharper end point in titrations
Sodium carbonate has a low molar mass, so weighing errors become very large
Solid NaOH absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, so its mass is unreliable
Solid NaOH is a weak base, so it reacts too slowly with acids to be useful
questions.explanation: A primary standard must be pure, stable and not absorb water or CO₂, so that a weighed mass gives an accurate amount. NaOH is a strong base but is hygroscopic and reacts with CO₂. A high molar mass, not a low one, reduces weighing error.

questions.stem: Why is the pH at the equivalence point above 7 when ethanoic acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide?
options: Excess sodium hydroxide is always present at the equivalence point in this titration
Ethanoic acid is diprotic, so the second proton reacts only after the equivalence point
Sodium ions react with water to produce hydroxide ions and hydrogen gas
The ethanoate ions formed are a weak base, which reacts with water to produce OH⁻
questions.explanation: At equivalence the flask holds sodium ethanoate. CH₃COO⁻ is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻ makes the solution slightly basic. Na⁺ does not react with water.

questions.stem: A student forgets to rinse the burette with the hydrochloric acid titrant, leaving it wet with water. How does this affect the calculated concentration of the base in the flask?
options: It is unaffected, because water does not react with the base
It is too high, because the diluted acid gives a larger titre
It is too low, because the diluted acid gives a larger titre
It is too high, because the diluted acid gives a smaller titre
questions.explanation: The water dilutes the acid, so more volume is needed to deliver the required moles. The calculation still uses the original acid concentration, so it overestimates the moles of acid added and therefore the concentration of the base.
